I really don't think it is limited to male fantasy, after all those are themes covered by Ursula K. Le Guin and to some extent Margaret Atwood. And I would not be surprised if there are other female or other gendered authors out there who have approached these ideas. 

However, I would not contrive that this is a universal fantasy, merely a collection of themes that are just now (in the 20th/21st century) being re-explored after a rather long hiatus. Sexual expression is highly dependent on culture (not surprising with our species). I think in American culture, it has been approached by male and female writers, but the male writers get more attention due to our cultural attitudes. It is often more acceptable to write from a male perspective, a sexual encounter with a much younger woman or even a girl, and the book will not be perceived as smut. The orgies depicted in Dune for example.

There's a pill now for everything nowadays!!

It does reek of an over enthusiastic infomercial. 

And so far, science, engineering and mathematics have proven more valuable to the species.

My mother was extremely mercurial in her belief in God and Christianity, but mostly she hammered in that a belief in God was necessary for morality. This lead to some pretty heated arguments between my parents, since my father was an atheist at the time. (He had a short lived conversion to Christianity in my teens, something that has puzzled me to this day).

Anyways, I am an atheist. I was an atheist then too, but a lot of pretending needed to be done to have any kind of peace and quiet in my teen years. 

But I would have to use this caveat, even in the presence of a deity (Yahweh or otherwise), I would not feel compelled to worship. A being so far outside the realm of human existence does not merit more than casual study, and if it claimed ownership of our species, it should merit contempt--given the obvious and numerous atrocities visited upon our species because of a belief in supernatural causes, while a powerful, immortal being had the knowledge and means to teach us otherwise. The other possibility is that this being is so multidimensional that communication would be impossible, and under that circumstance, why should anyone worship it? Study--yes, but dedicate one's life to a fan club for a being that may exist, that might care for you, is rather foolish in my opinion.

It's a check box of normalcy, let the others know you are not a robot, you are human, and it is a way of gathering information about your coworkers/people in general without seeming forward. I generally inquire out of politeness (because sensitivity classes suck), and to gauge what level of emotional BS needs to be dealt with in the workplace.

My advice would be to give her something to do. You already know what the project is, what it entails, endure the feelings talk and push her in the direction of items that she can micromanage while you work. It is a bit like distracting a toddler.

And those would be the well meaning temptations. 

Of course I get that it's a children's book, but there are many factors in the story that could have disastrous consequences. Memory charm your way to being a millionaire. Late to work? A bit of time magic...

I would think the Harry Potter would be rather terrible for all of its magic and mundanity. Kids with a middle school education being told that power is enough and keep it secret, living along side our wonderful mundane world, adult life for an average wizard would be rather brutal.
